papers.title: Proteomics identified carboxypeptidase E as a novel biomarker for synucleinopathies.
papers.abstract: Aggregated alpha-synuclein (α-syn) forms Lewy bodies (LBs) in neurons in Parkinson's disease (PD) and glial cytoplasmic inclusions (GCIs) in oligodendrocytes in Multiple System Atrophy (MSA). However, the molecular composition of these inclusions and the molecular features associated with different synucleinopathy-related inclusion types remain incompletely understood. Here, we characterized α-syn-positive inclusion bodies across disease-relevant brain regions using spatial proteomics in postmortem PD and MSA brains. Comparative analysis identified 614 proteins shared between LB and GCI proteomes, including 57 proteins showing differential enrichment between the two inclusion types. Among these, carboxypeptidase E (CPE) exhibited significant co-aggregation with α-syn in both PD and MSA brains. We further quantified serum CPE levels by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay in a discovery cohort (66 PD, 37 MSA, and 23 non-neurodegenerative controls [NNCs]) and a salivary α-syn real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC)-positive cohort (26 PD, 14 MSA, and 22 NNCs). Serum CPE levels were significantly reduced in synucleinopathy patients compared with controls and showed robust diagnostic performance across both cohorts. Lower CPE levels were inversely correlated with selected markers of clinical disease severity. These findings identify CPE as a co-aggregated protein associated with α-syn-positive inclusions and support its further evaluation as a candidate biomarker for synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Machine-learning-assisted CRISPR/Cas12a biosensing for biomarker identification of neurodegenerative movement disorders.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative movement disorders (NMDs) such as Parkinson's disease (PD), progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) and multiple system atrophy (MSA) share overlapping clinical features yet distinct pathology, complicating early diagnosis. We present a machine-learning-assisted, glass-fiber-based CRISPR-Cas12a immunosensing platform (GUSCI) for multiplexed quantification of five extracellular-vesicle (EV) biomarkers in paired serum and serum-derived CD81⁺ EVs. Across 340 clinical samples, integrated EV biomarker profiles supported exploratory classification analyses and generally showed stronger discriminatory signals than matched serum markers. EV-derived 4R Tau enabled discrimination of PSP (AUC = 0.848 (95% CI 0.7379-0.9362)), whereas combined EV signatures of IL-6, TNF-α and α-synuclein distinguished PD (AUC = 0.823 (95% CI 0.7185-0.8988)). These findings support serum-derived EV biomarker profiling by GUSCI as a promising exploratory framework for biomarker discovery and differential diagnosis in NMDs.

papers.title: Impaired effort perception, not reward sensitivity, impacts the effort-reward trade-off in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Deciding whether and how to act depends on a trade-off between the effort required to execute a given action and the potential reward for completing it. Impairments in this effort-reward trade-off have been proposed to underlie reduced movement vigor, or bradykinesia, in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, several mechanisms could alter the effort-reward trade-off in PD, each with unique implications for understanding and treating bradykinesia. Therefore, we individually examined whether people with PD (both on and off dopamine medication) demonstrated reduced sensitivity to reward value, increased perception of effort, or a biased mapping between effort and reward, compared to age- and sex-matched neurotypical controls. We found that people with PD exhibited increased effort perception and, surprisingly, no reduced sensitivity to reward value or a biased mapping between effort and reward. These findings suggest that effort perception could be an important factor driving bradykinesia in PD.

papers.title: Basal forebrain atrophy links short-latency afferent inhibition to cognition in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease is closely associated with degeneration of the cholinergic system, yet the precise structure-function relationships underlying this link remain incompletely characterized. Short-latency afferent inhibition (SAI) is a widely used neurophysiological marker of cholinergic circuit integrity, but its specific anatomical substrate and relationship to domain-specific cognitive decline are not fully elucidated. This study integrated neurophysiology, structural MRI and cognitive data to characterize the association between cholinergic basal forebrain (cBF) atrophy, SAI and cognitive performance in Parkinson's disease. In this cross-sectional study, we enrolled 119 patients with Parkinson's disease spanning the cognitive continuum from normal cognition to dementia (mean age 63.9 ± 9 years) and 32 healthy controls. All participants underwent assessment of SAI and multimodal MRI for automated volumetry of anterior and posterior basal forebrain subregions and substantia nigra free-water mapping. Cognitive status was classified using the Parkinson's Disease Cognitive Rating Scale (PD-CRS), yielding scores for global cognition and fronto-subcortical and posterior-cortical functions. Regression models and bootstrap mediation analysis were used to examine the SAI-cognition association and decompose it into components shared with and independent of the cBF volume. SAI was reduced in patients compared with controls. Within the PD group, after adjustment for clinically relevant covariates, SAI was significantly associated with PD-CRS total (β = -0.19, P = 0.013) and posterior-cortical scores (β = -0.44, P < 0.001), but not with the fronto-subcortical score (β = -0.13, P = 0.103). papers.title: Vestibular implant as a novel peripheral neuromodulation strategy for complex movement disorders. A pilot study in patients with Parkinson's disease associated with bilateral vestibular dysfunction.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is increasingly recognized as a disorder of distributed sensorimotor networks, in which axial symptoms such as gait impairment and postural instability frequently become refractory to conventional therapies. The vestibular system provides continuous input to basal ganglia, cerebellar, thalamic, and cortical pathways involved in motor control, representing a potential target for peripheral neuromodulation. This study investigates the effects of chronic vestibular implant (VI) stimulation in patients with PD and concomitant bilateral vestibular hypofunction (BVP). METHODS: Six patients received a VI, including three patients with PD-associated BVP. All participants were prospectively evaluated before implantation and 12 months after device activation. Outcomes were compared with a matched cohort of three patients with isolated BVP receiving the same implant. Motor results were assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale part III (MDS-UPDRS III), together with dynamic balance, quality-of-life measures, comprehensive vestibular testing, and dopaminergic neuroimaging using 123I RESULTS: All patients with PD-associated BVP demonstrated clinically relevant motor improvement following VI activation, with MDS-UPDRS III reductions of 45, 20, and 27 points, respectively. The most consistent improvements involved bradykinesia, gait, freezing of gait, and postural stability, whereas tremor-related items showed a more variable response. Dynamic balance and sensory integration improved after implantation, with functional outcomes approaching those observed in patients with isolated BVP. These preliminary findings support vestibular implantat

papers.title: Association of baseline dopamine transporter binding with early clinical stage transitions and functional milestones in individuals at risk for Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early progression in individuals at risk for Parkinson's disease (PD) can involve both emerging symptoms and changes in daily function. Identifying baseline markers associated with these changes could inform longitudinal assessment and risk stratification. Although lower dopamine transporter (DAT) binding has been linked to clinical conversion, its relationship with early clinical stage transitions and functional milestones across different PD risk populations remains unclear. METHODS: Using prospectively collected data from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative, we studied 1,696 GBA1 or LRRK2 variant carriers and individuals with isolated rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder or hyposmia. Adjusted cause-specific Cox models assessed baseline putaminal DAT binding in relation to first clinical stage progression and functional milestones over three years. Additional analyses evaluated α-synuclein seed amplification assay (SAA) status and baseline clinical stage. RESULTS: Lower DAT-binding was linked to higher stage-progression hazard, with a steeper gradient at lower values (Holm-adjusted P < 0.001; unadjusted nonlinearity P = 0.020). Each 0.5-unit lower specific binding ratio corresponded to a higher hazard of first attainment of functional impairment (hazard ratio [HR] 1.55, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.26-1.90). Milestone hazard was higher at baseline stage ≥ 3 than stage 2 (HR 3.14, 95% CI 2.30-4.29). DAT binding was not significantly associated with milestones. SAA positivity showed no significant relationship with stage progression or milestones. CONCLUSIONS: These findings link baseline DAT binding to early clinical stage transitions and baseline functional impairment to subsequent milestones, supporting further evaluation of both measures for risk stratification in longitudinal studies.

papers.title: Beyond Total Homocysteine: Context-Specific Biomarker Roles and Molecular Phenotypes Across Vascular and Neurological Disorders.
papers.abstract: Plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) is analytically mature, but its clinical meaning depends on the question the test is intended to answer. This narrative review interprets homocysteine as a context-specific biomarker using the FDA-NIH BEST (Biomarkers, EndpointS, and other Tools) framework, distinguishing susceptibility/risk, diagnostic, prognostic, monitoring, pharmacodynamic, and surrogate-endpoint uses, together with the pre-analytical, renal, nutritional, and pharmacological determinants of routine results. tHcy has established clinical utility as a diagnostic-pathway and monitoring marker in severe inherited homocysteine disorders. In vascular disease, stroke, and cognitive decline, it is a nonspecific susceptibility or prognostic marker, and in selected levodopa- or antiseizure-medication users, a candidate treatment-associated monitoring marker. It is not a diagnostic biomarker for Alzheimer's or Parkinson's disease, and reliable biochemical lowering by B vitamins has not translated consistently into clinical benefit, so it is not a qualified surrogate endpoint. We propose five molecular homocysteine phenotypes-remethylation-deficient, transsulfuration-deficient, renal-retention, treatment-related methylation, and protein-modification-as a hypothesis-generating conceptual framework that has not been empirically validated. Each phenotype is specified by routine measurements and exploratory analytes; S-adenosylmethionine, S-adenosylhomocysteine, homocysteine-thiolactone, and N-homocysteinylated proteins remain research tools. A tiered testing framework and a staged validation roadmap are proposed, both requiring prospective evaluation before clinical implementation.

papers.title: A Computational Investigation of Curcumin Glucoside in α-Synuclein Aggregation: DFT Characterization, Molecular Docking, and Secondary Data Analysis.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the aggregation of α-synuclein into oligomers and amyloid fibrils. Curcumin glucoside has been investigated as a potential inhibitor of α-synuclein aggregation; however, understanding its electronic properties and predicted interactions with α-synuclein fibrils may provide additional insights into its potential molecular behavior. This study integrates density functional theory (DFT) calculations, molecular docking, and quantitative analysis of previously published Thioflavin-T (ThT) fluorescence data to investigate the physicochemical properties and potential anti-aggregation effects of curcumin glucoside. DFT calculations were performed on isolated curcumin and curcumin monoglucoside molecules using the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/def2-SVP level of theory with implicit aqueous solvation. The HOMO-LUMO energy gaps were 3.626 eV for curcumin and 3.372 eV for curcumin monoglucoside, while their dipole moments were 7.53 D and 11.19 D, respectively. These differences indicate changes in the electronic structure and molecular polarity associated with glucosylation. Molecular docking against selected α-synuclein fibril structures representing different disease stages showed docking scores ranging from -5.1 to -6.7 kcal/mol for curcumin and from -6.2 to -6.6 kcal/mol for curcumin glucoside. Previously published ThT fluorescence data related to curcumin glucoside were analyzed using a four-parameter logistic (4PL) model to characterize the reported aggregation-response profiles over time. The combined findings provide complementary electronic-structure, docking, and aggregation-kinetic perspectives on curcumin glucoside. Importantly, the DFT calculations were restricted to isolated molecules and did not evaluate electron redistribution, charge-transfer pathways, or reaction energetics within protein-ligand complexes. papers.title: Telomeres, Aging and Neurodegenerative Diseases: Molecular Mechanisms, Clinical Evidence and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Telomeres are regions located at the ends of chromosomes, consisting of tandemly repeated nucleotide sequences. Their primary functions are to protect chromosome ends, prevent the recognition of natural chromosome termini as DNA double-strand breaks and contribute to the regulation of cellular replicative capacity. Indeed, with each cell division cycle, they shorten until reaching a critical threshold that signals the cell to stop replicating, a process known as "cellular senescence". Telomere shortening also occurs in response to oxidative stress and DNA damage; several studies have reported an association between shorter telomere length and neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), and dementia-related outcomes. However, findings are heterogeneous, and the relationship between telomere length and cognitive or functional decline remains incompletely understood. Telomere dysfunction may also affect glial cell function, potentially contributing to chronic neuroinflammation and the release of pro-inflammatory molecules. This process increases neuronal vulnerability. Several studies suggest that telomere damage may influence the neurotoxicity caused by β-amyloid oligomers and accelerate neurodegenerative processes. Furthermore, in experimental models, interventions targeting telomerase, the enzyme that preserves DNA integrity by lengthening lost telomere repeats, have shown potential therapeutic promise. However, the relationship between telomere shortening and disease progression is still unclear, and telomere length cannot even be considered a clinically applicable predictive biomarker. Although telomere shortening is a marker of biological aging and a potential factor in the pathogenesis of neurodegenerative diseases, large-scale longitudinal studies and interventional trials are needed to consider telomeres as biomarkers and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Molecularly Aged Protein States as Targets for Drug Design and Delivery in Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative drug discovery usually represents a protein target by its gene, canonical sequence, and one or a few structures. That representation can miss the molecular history accumulated by proteins that persist in the brain. Spontaneous chemistry, incomplete repair, altered turnover, proteolysis, phase transitions, and assembly remodeling generate states that may differ from the canonical target in exposure, function, and therapeutic accessibility. We call compositionally resolved species age-generated proteoforms and use molecularly aged protein states when the exact composition remains uncertain. This Review develops a target-state framework for Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia, Huntington disease, and multiple sclerosis. It separates detection from age association, causality, brain exposure, proximal target engagement, and clinical evidence. Disease-specific analyses connect tau and amyloid-beta proteoforms, alpha-synuclein and lysosomal or mitochondrial assemblies, TDP-43 loss-of-function states, and persistent myelin or extracellular-matrix states to rational modalities and critical validation experiments. Repair, selective removal, stabilization, state-selective antibodies and small molecules, intrabodies, replacement, and synthesis control are evaluated together with blood-brain barrier transport, cellular and organelle access, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics. Each class of target state is mapped to the delivery constraint it imposes and the platform for which a precedent exists, and the exposure requirements that state selectivity implies are set out explicitly, including the fraction of a pool that must be engaged, the duration required to move a slowly accumulating state, and the consequences for dosing interval and pharmacodynamic biomarker choice. papers.title: Molecular understanding of liquid-liquid phase separation of α-synuclein for the development of novel Parkinson's disease therapies.
papers.abstract: α-Synuclein (α-syn) exists abundantly at presynaptic terminals and plays a pivotal role in vesicle trafficking and neurotransmitter release thereafter. α-Syn exhibits structural plasticity and adopts diverse conformations such as α-helices and β-strands in response to adjacent microenvironments. These structural features facilitate the formation of aberrant α-syn condensates under specific circumstances. Aggregates and amyloid fibrils of α-syn have been observed in the brain tissue of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) and other synucleinopathies. Τhe nucleation of α-syn as a precursor to aggregation and amyloid formation is associated with liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS), which forms droplets in solution. Thus, elucidating the detailed molecular formation of α-syn LLPS is necessary to understand the aberrant polymerization of α-syn, such as the formation of amyloid fibrils. In this review, we describe the formation mechanism of α-syn LLPS. In addition, we discuss several molecular strategies for targeting α-syn LLPS to block the formation of α-syn aggregates or amyloid fibrils. This review provides biophysical insights for the development of novel therapies for PD.

papers.title: Research Advances on Gut-Brain Axis in Parkinson's Disease Pathogenesis and Prodromal Prediction.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's Disease (PD) is a common chronic progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Traditionally, it has been considered to be a disorder confined to dopaminergic neuronal injury in the substantia nigra of the central nervous system. However, increasing evidence from epidemiology, clinical imaging, and molecular biology suggests that the pathological process of PD may begin in the gut, with the gut-brain axis participating in disease initiation and progression. This review systematically summarizes the structural and physiological regulatory mechanisms of the gut-brain axis, focusing in particular on the aggregation of α-synuclein in the gut and its prion-like propagation, features of gut microbiota dysbiosis, leaky gut and systemic inflammatory cascades, and vagus nerve-related transmission mechanisms. Centering on prodromal PD, we discuss in depth early biomarkers based on this framework and propose a multi-dimensional combinatorial strategy integrating gut microbiota, barrier-related molecules and prodromal clinical phenotypes, to provide new perspectives for the prodromal prediction of PD.

The nanobody PFFNB2 inhibits α-syn pre-formed fibrils (α-syn PFF) but faces expression challenges due to the absence of a canonical disulfide bond. papers.title: Strategies for untangling protein amyloid aggregates.
papers.abstract: Disruption in protein folding might lead to the formation of structured protein aggregates called amyloids. The accumulation of amyloid in tissues, termed amyloidosis, is correlated with various diseases, including Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and systemic amyloidosis. Therefore, understanding the mechanisms of protein aggregation into fibrils and the disintegration of mature fibrils is necessary for the development of therapeutic strategies against these diseases. While protein aggregation and its inhibition are relatively well studied, disaggregation of protein amyloids remains underexplored due to the difficulties inherent in disrupting these highly stable structures. In this review, we have discussed the challenges associated with fibril disaggregation and current strategies to disrupt fibrils formed by Aβ-42, tau, α-synuclein, and insulin, which are implicated in amyloidogenic disorders. In particular, we emphasize fibril disaggregation using small molecules, chaperones, nanoparticles, and peptides, highlighting their modes of action and potential strategies for developing therapeutic molecules for translational applications.

papers.title: Phytochemicals as Modulators of Biomolecular Condensates and Liquid-Liquid Phase Separation in Neurodegenerative Diseases: Emerging Mechanisms and Therapeutic Perspectives.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are increasingly recognized as disorders of cellular proteostasis characterized by progressive protein imbalance, defective stress adaptation, and neuronal dysfunction. Recent discoveries have established biomolecular condensates generated through liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) as essential regulators of neuronal organization, coordinating RNA metabolism, protein quality control, stress responses, and intracellular signaling. Alterations in condensate composition, material properties, and turnover are now considered important contributors to the conversion of physiological protein assemblies into persistent pathological structures, thereby influencing the progression of Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, frontotemporal dementia, and related disorders. Natural compounds, including polyphenols, flavonoids, and other phytochemicals, have gained increasing attention due to their broad neuroprotective activities; however, their potential ability to influence condensate biology remains incompletely characterized. This review provides a comprehensive and critical analysis of current evidence connecting natural compounds with biomolecular condensate homeostasis, including direct effects on phase separation as well as indirect regulation through stress granule remodeling, molecular chaperone activity, autophagy, mitochondrial function, oxidative balance, neuroinflammatory pathways, and proteostasis networks. Particular emphasis is placed on the molecular mechanisms through which these bioactive molecules may affect aggregation-associated pathways involving amyloid-β, tau, α-synuclein, TDP-43, and FUS. Finally, current experimental limitations, translational challenges, and future perspectives are discussed, highlighting biomolecular condensates as emerging therapeutic targets and natural compounds as potential multimodal modulators capable of preserving physiological phase behavior while limi

papers.title: Cellular, Lipid, and Metabolic Dysregulation in LRRK2-Driven Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: This review highlights the emerging association of LRRK2 with lipid homeostasis and cellular metabolism, suggesting the therapeutic potential of these pathways in LRRK2-driven Parkinson's Disease. Recent findings indicate that LRRK2 regulates Rab GTPases through phosphorylation events and may also orchestrate organelle metabolism critical for cellular homeostasis. LRRK2 mutations have been shown to cause lipid and metabolic imbalance, which may contribute to pathogenic α-Synuclein (α-Syn) aggregation and subsequent neurodegeneration. Multiomic studies, largely in idiopathic PD, support these connections; however, analyses of LRRK2-PD postmortem brain tissues are still limited. While brain-penetrant LRRK2 kinase inhibitors have recently advanced to mid-phase clinical trials, abnormalities downstream of LRRK2 functions remain prime therapeutic targets. Collectively, mechanistic and omics-based evidence suggests that targeting metabolic and lipid dysregulation may complement LRRK2 kinase inhibition.

papers.title: Imaging Transcriptomic Signatures Associated with Brain Atrophy Across Clinical Subtypes of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) motor subtypes, tremor-dominant (TD) and postural instability/gait difficulty (PIGD), exhibit divergent brain atrophy patterns, yet the transcriptomic basis of this subtype-associated vulnerability remains incompletely understood. We employed an integrative imaging transcriptomics approach to identify both different and shared transcriptomic signatures associated with regional gray matter volume in PD and its clinical subtypes (TD and PIGD). METHODS: Ninety-nine PD patients (50 TD, 47 PIGD, 2 indeterminate) and 70 healthy controls (HCs) underwent 3T MRI, regional gray matter volume differences were assessed between PD subtypes and HCs. Partial least squares (PLS) regression linked atrophy patterns to Allen Human Brain Atlas gene expression across brain regions, followed by functional enrichment, pathology-related gene enrichment, cell-type enrichment, and neurotransmitter system mapping. RESULTS: PIGD and TD showed partially overlapping atrophy patterns, with relatively greater cortical and subcortical involvement in PIGD and a narrower pattern in TD. PLS identified 78 shared and hundreds of subtype-associated genes. PIGD-associated genes were tentatively enriched in synaptic pathways and overlapped significantly with alpha-synuclein pathology-related genes, while TD-associated genes were enriched in chromatin regulation and proteostasis. Neurotransmitter mapping revealed broad neurotransmitter involvement in PIGD versus more restricted dominance in TD. CONCLUSIONS: PD subtypes exhibit both shared and subtype-associated transcriptomic signatures underlying regional atrophy vulnerability, with PIGD showing relatively more pronounced synaptic disruption and broader neurotransmitter involvement. These findings shed light on the molecular underpinnings that may contribute to the heterogeneity of disease distribution in PD clinical subtypes and may inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Beyond Baseline: Symptom Trajectories and Prognostic Associations of Complementary Therapies in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Parkinson's disease (PD) progression is highly heterogeneous, and prognostic biomarkers guiding personalized management remain elusive. Complementary therapies are widely used by people with PD. Their real-world associations with long-term symptom progression remain poorly characterized, and conclusions drawn from observational data depend on the analytic approach used. We examined baseline complementary therapy use in relation to symptom severity and its rate of change using four complementary analytic approaches. METHODS: Data came from the Modifiable Variables in Parkinsonism prospective cohort study (2013-present, n RESULTS: Vitamin D (63.1%), vitamin B12 (40.6%), and fish oil (39.5%) were most frequently used. In the full 24-therapy baseline model, low-dose lithium, fish oil, and coenzyme Q10 were associated with lower baseline symptom severity, whereas oral glutathione was borderline (p CONCLUSIONS: Associations between complementary therapy use and PD symptoms depended strongly on the analytic approach, and cross-sectional associations were a poor guide to later symptom change. Long-term pragmatic follow-up identified over-the-counter therapies associated with slower (oral glutathione, coconut oil) and faster (NAC, probiotics) symptom accumulation. These findings do not establish causation; rather, they illustrate the value of systematically examining longitudinal patient-reported data in identifying biologically plausible patterns that emerge amid the complexity of real-world care and can guide subsequent explanatory research.

papers.title: A Pre-post Rehabilitation Study of Exosomal mRNA and lncRNA Expression Profiles Reveals Potential Role of UBE2G1 in Rehabilitation of Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Journal of central nervous system disease
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) and messenger RNAs (mRNAs) are implicated in the development and progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). This study aims to examine the potential of any lncRNA as biomarkers underlying PD rehabilitation. METHODS: Pre-post rehabilitation study of lncRNA and mRNA expression profiles may identify the potential biomarkers associated with rehabilitation. We enrolled 6 patients with PD (PWP) and 6 age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HCs) in this study. Peripheral blood samples were collected before and after 14-day rehabilitation treatment to extract total RNA from exosomes. Differentially expressed mRNAs (DEmRNAs) and differentially expressed lncRNAs (DElncRNAs) were identified by next-generation sequencing (NGS). A co-expression network was built. RESULTS: Overall, pre-post rehabilitation study of exosomal mRNA revealed 1,662 DEmRNAs (606 upregulated and 1,056 downregulated) in PWPs. Compared with the HCs, 1,723 DElncRNAs (1,278 upregulated and 445 downregulated lncRNAs) and 1,931 DElncRNAs (1,561 upregulated and 370 downregulated) were identified in the blood exosomes of pre-rehab and post-rehab PWPs, respectively. GO and KEEG enrichment analyses revealed significant enrichment of proteasome-mediated ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process, and ubiquitin mediated proteolysis pathways, suggesting their potential role in the progression of PD. Co-expression network analysis identified one DElncRNA (ENST00000421331) and one positively related DEmRNA (ENSG00000132388, UBE2G1). The preliminary findings suggest that UBE2G1 is implicated in PD rehabilitation. papers.title: ApoE4 and Psychosis in Neurodegenerative and Non-Neurodegenerative Disease: A Scoping Review.
papers.abstract: Psychosis is a neuropsychiatric feature found across neurodegenerative conditions including Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD). It is also a common feature in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia. The apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 (ApoE4) allele is an established genetic risk factor for AD that may also increase the risk of psychosis. However, evidence regarding the association between ApoE4 and psychosis remains unclear. This paper evaluates the relationship between ApoE4 carrier status and psychosis in both neurodegenerative (Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease) and non-neurodegenerative disorders (schizophrenia). Additionally it explores whether sex and zygosity modulate this association. A literature review of studies identified through PubMed and Scopus was conducted. papers.title: Social Isolation Aggravates Depression-like Behavior in Rotenone-Induced Parkinson's Disease Mice by Disrupting the Gut-Microbiota-Brain Axis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with a rising global burden. Depression is one of the most common non-motor manifestations of PD and substantially worsens daily functions and disease prognosis. Social isolation (SI) is a common but underrecognized psychosocial stressor in PD patients due to motor impairments like resting tremor and abnormal gait; however, the mechanisms linking SI to depression aggravation are unclear. Considering the emerging role of the gut-microbiota-brain axis in PD development, intestinal homeostasis, neuroinflammation, and neuropsychiatric regulation, we investigated whether gut microbiota dysbiosis is implicated in depression-like behaviors aggravated by SI in a rotenone-induced mouse model of PD. METHODS: A rotenone-induced PD mouse model was combined with SI. Depression-like behaviors, dopaminergic neuronal integrity, neurochemical alterations, serum corticosterone, intestinal inflammation, gut-barrier function, and gut microbial composition were assessed using behavioral tests, immunohistochemistry, biochemical assays, histological and molecular analyses, and 16S rRNA sequencing. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) was conducted to examine whether microbiota from socially isolated PD mice could transfer related behavioral and pathological phenotypes to recipient mice. RESULTS: SI significantly aggravated depression-like behaviors in rotenone-treated mice, along with further reduction in tyrosine hydroxylase-positive cells in the substantia nigra, lower hippocampal 5-hydroxytryptamine and brain-derived neurotrophic factor levels, and elevated serum corticosterone. SI also promoted intestinal inflammation and impaired gut-barrier integrity in PD mice. 16S rRNA sequencing demonstrated that SI reduced the alpha diversity of gut microbiota and altered microbial community composition. papers.title: Distinct Fractional Amplitude of Low-Frequency Fluctuation in Parkinson's Disease Patients with Comorbid Anxiety and Depression: A Resting-State fMRI Study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Anxiety and depression symptoms are prevalent and persistent in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). Most neuroimaging studies have examined PD patients presenting with isolated anxiety or depression, whereas few studies have specifically investigated patients with concurrent anxiety and depression, a clinically more severe subtype. The present study therefore sought to unravel the neural mechanisms underlying PD with comorbid anxiety and depression (PD-A&D). METHODS: This study enrolled 35 PD-A&D patients, 32 PD patients without anxiety and depression (PD), and 38 healthy control subjects (HCs), who underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging using a 3.0T scanner. Fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) analysis was used to assess spontaneous brain activity across the three groups. Correlations between fALFF alterations and the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HAMA) as well as the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD) scores were examined within the PD-A&D group. RESULTS: Relative to the PD group, PD-A&D patients exhibited significant fALFF reductions primarily in the right putamen/caudate, right superior frontal gyrus, right precuneus, and right inferior parietal lobe. Furthermore, relative to HCs, PD-A&D patients displayed widespread fALFF alterations in the left cerebellar Crus I/lobule VI, left precuneus and so on. These findings provide preliminary and exploratory insights into the neural heterogeneity of PD-A&D patients. papers.title: Clozapine beyond schizophrenia: an umbrella systematic review of the off-label uses of clozapine in managing psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To systematically appraise the literature for systematic reviews on the off-label uses of clozapine for psychiatric, neurological, and behavioural conditions beyond psychotic disorders. METHODS: Systematic searches of Medline, PsychInfo, CINAHL, and Cochrane Database were performed on February 8th, 2025, using the search terms "clozapine" AND "systematic review". Systematic reviews investigating clozapine as an intervention for conditions aside from schizophrenia (or related psychotic disorders) were included in this review. Risk of bias was assessed using the AMSTAR 2 assessment tool. FINDINGS: The search yielded 571 studies after removal of duplicates, with 20 studies being suitable for systematic review. Six meta-analyses were found to meet the inclusion criteria demonstrating clozapine's efficacy in managing Parkinson's psychosis (SMD = -4.23; 95% CI = -6.53, -1.93), tardive dyskinesia (SMD = - 2.56, p = 0.02), insomnia (OR = 0.45, p < 0.01), substance use disorder (OR = 0.10, p < 0.00001), and in reducing suicidality (OR = 0.229, p < 0.0001) and mortality (RR = 0.43, 95% CI = 0.34-0.55). Additionally, systematic reviews were found meeting the inclusion criteria demonstrating that clozapine was efficacious in managing treatment-resistant bipolar disorder, borderline personality disorder, catatonia, psychogenic polydipsia, essential tremor, behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD), neurodevelopmental disorders, violence and aggression, and aggression in children. Confidence in the quality of evidence was assessed to be high in 7, moderate in 3, low in 3, and critically low in 7 reviews. CONCLUSIONS: Clozapine is potentially efficacious in the off-label management of a wide range of psychiatric and neurological conditions beyond treatment-resistant schizophrenia. papers.title: Association of subthalamic deep brain stimulation programming parameters with cognitive trajectories in Parkinson's disease.
papers.journal: Neurotherapeutics : the journal of the American Society for Experimental NeuroTherapeutics
papers.abstract: High-frequency deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the subthalamic nucleus (STN) is an effective therapy for motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD). However, its impact on cognition remains debated. This retrospective, observational study of 78 consecutive PD patients who underwent bilateral STN-DBS aimed to investigate the association between STN-DBS parameter settings (pulse width, amplitude, and frequency) and cognitive outcomes over twelve months in PD, as well as their link to motor functioning. Among the evaluated DBS programming parameters, pulse width emerged as the only factor consistently associated with longitudinal cognitive trajectories. This association remained robust across multiple sensitivity analyses, including patient-level and motor-adjusted models, whereas amplitude and frequency showed no significant relationships with cognition. Patients with pulse widths <60 μs showed a greater likelihood of cognitive decline compared to those with standard (60 μs) or longer widths. Our results suggest that pulse width may represent an underrecognized determinant of cognitive outcomes following STN-DBS and support its consideration in future prospective studies aimed at optimizing DBS programming beyond motor symptoms alone.

papers.title: An IoT-Based Healthcare Monitoring and Surveillance Framework for People with Special Needs.
papers.abstract: People with special needs, such as frail older adults and people living with Parkinson's disease (PD), heart-rhythm disorders or dementia, are often alone when a critical event happens. We present IoT-CARES, a four-layer Internet of Things (IoT) framework with one lightweight edge pipeline for five services: fall detection, activity monitoring of adults aged 70+, freezing-of-gait (FoG) detection, single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) arrhythmia monitoring and camera-free cognitive-health surveillance. A dual-view ensemble (a fixed average of gradient-boosted trees on physiological descriptors and a linear model on random-convolution features) runs without a deep-learning runtime. A subject-level conformal calibration bounds a new person's false-alarm rate by a carer-chosen budget with probability ≥90%, provided that new and calibration people are exchangeable, and federated learning trains shared models without moving raw data. On five open datasets (438 people), evaluated on held-out people, the framework reached an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.9998 for simulated falls and 0.908 for FoG, and a macro-F1 of 0.778 for activity; federated training matched centralised training. Personalisation helped only when the onboarding data contained the target events: five labelled ECG minutes raised arrhythmia macro-F1 from 0.667 (best global model) to 0.932, whereas fine-tuning on routine activity lowered activity macro-F1 (0.766 to 0.683) unless only the output layer was adapted (0.795). Conformal calibration kept 16 of 17 young volunteers (94.1%; 95% confidence interval 71.3-99.9%) free of false fall alarms during their activity protocol while detecting 94.6% of simulated falls (window-optimal threshold: 76.5% free of false alarms), and kept 9 of 10 people with PD within four false cues per hour; with so few people, these estimates are imprecise. In free-living data of 18 adults aged 70-95 years, a fall threshold calibrated on the v

papers.title: Trans-Spinal Theta Burst Stimulation for Persistent Gait Dysfunction in Parkinson's Disease After Deep Brain Stimulation: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Trial.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Axial symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD) are challenging to treat, even with deep brain stimulation (DBS). Trans-spinal magnetic stimulation (TsMS) has emerged as a potential neuromodulatory approach for gait and balance dysfunction. METHODS: In this randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial, patients with PD treated with subthalamic or pallidal DBS received active or sham TsMS (intermittent theta burst stimulation over the third thoracic vertebra, one session per day) for five consecutive days. The primary outcome was gait performance measured by the Timed Up and Go (TUG) test at day 28 (week 4) after the final stimulation session. Secondary outcomes included balance (Balance Evaluation Systems Test, BESTest), freezing of gait, motor severity (Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale, part III, MDS-UPDRS-III), and quality of life scales. RESULTS: Thirty-nine patients were randomized (19 active, 20 sham) and included in the analysis. No significant difference was observed in TUG at the prespecified primary follow-up at week 4 (p CONCLUSIONS: Trans-spinal theta burst stimulation did not improve gait, freezing, motor severity or quality of life compared with sham. Small transient changes observed in isolated balance subdomains were exploratory, were not sustained over time, and should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Association of Peri-Lead Air Cavity With Acute Symptomatic Peri-Lead Edema and Long-Term Clinical Outcomes Following Subthalamic Nucleus Deep Brain Stimulation in Parkinson Disease.
papers.journal: Neuromodulation : journal of the International Neuromodulation Society
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Symptomatic peri-lead edema (PLE) is an uncommon complication of deep brain stimulation (DBS) that may mimic infection, hemorrhage, or infarction. Its acute radiologic characteristics remain poorly defined, and its long-term clinical outcomes are uncertain. We characterized the acute radiologic features of symptomatic PLE after bilateral subthalamic nucleus DBS for Parkinson disease, with particular focus on peri-lead air, and evaluated long-term outcomes. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We retrospectively studied 372 consecutive patients who underwent single-stage bilateral subthalamic nucleus DBS between October 2005 and December 2025. Symptomatic PLE was defined as new neurologic symptoms occurring within seven days accompanied by new peri-lead edema on computed tomography (CT) without hemorrhage. Peri-lead air was quantified on immediate postoperative and follow-up CT and compared with radiologic controls. Long-term outcomes through 24 months were compared with propensity score-matched controls. RESULTS: A total of 22 of 372 patients (5.9%) developed symptomatic PLE. A focal peri-lead air cavity was identified in 18 (82%) of these patients compared with one of 31 radiologic controls (3%; p < 0.001). Peri-lead air volume increased from immediate postoperative to follow-up CT in patients with PLE (median, 0.20 vs 0.54 mL; p < 0.001) but decreased in controls. Air volume correlated with edema cross-sectional area (Spearman ρ = 0.64; p < 0.001). Among the 20 patients with one-month CT available, edema resolved in 17 (85%), and all patients recovered without permanent neurologic deficits. No significant differences in long-term clinical outcomes were detected between patients with symptomatic PLE and their matched controls. CONCLUSIONS: Symptomatic PLE was associated with a focal peri-lead air cavity that persisted or increased during the acute postoperative period, although its temporal and causal relationship with edema remains uncertain. papers.title: Progressive Fatigue-Related Gait Changes During Continuous Walking in Parkinson's Disease: A Repeated Motion Capture Assessment.
papers.abstract: Fatigue is one of the most prevalent and disabling non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), contributing to mobility limitations. Previous studies have mainly used pre-post assessment paradigms, providing limited information on how gait changes progressively as fatigue increases. This study investigated the association between increasing lower-limb perceived exertion and gait biomechanics during continuous walking in PD. Thirty-seven participants underwent repeated instrumented gait assessments while walking at the fastest sustainable speed until reaching a Borg Rating of Perceived Exertion for the lower limbs (RPE-LL) of 17. Linear mixed-effects models were used to examine the association between RPE-LL and spatiotemporal, kinematic, kinetic, and COM displacement parameters. Increasing perceived exertion was significantly associated with reduced gait speed, cadence, peak hip extension, and ankle push-off power, together with increased double-support time, mediolateral center-of-mass displacement during double support, trunk sagittal inclination, and knee flexion during single support. Exploratory analyses suggested that selected motor impairments modulate fatigue-related gait adaptations. These findings show that progressively increasing perceived exertion is associated with widespread gait deterioration during prolonged walking in PD. Repeated instrumented gait assessment provides a framework for characterizing fatigue as a dynamic process and supports the development of personalized rehabilitation strategies.

papers.title: Dynamical Analysis of Abnormal Oscillatory Activity in the BG and PPN Associated with Sleep-Related Alterations in Parkinson's Disease and Its Modulation by DBS.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common neurodegenerative disorder in which over 80% of patients experience severe sleep disorders. Understanding the neural dynamical mechanisms underlying these sleep disturbances is essential for developing targeted therapeutic strategies. METHODS: We construct a basal ganglia-thalamocortical-pedunculopontine nucleus (BGTC-PPN) network model by combining Hodgkin-Huxley and Izhikevich neuron models to simulate both healthy and PD network dynamics. We systematically compare the discharge patterns, synchronization indices and power spectral densities of key nuclei between healthy and PD conditions. In addition, we use coherence analysis to characterize the frequency-dependent coupling between the PPN and basal ganglia nuclei, and investigate deep brain stimulation (DBS) modulation effects on the PD network using rectangular-wave stimulation at three target nuclei. RESULTS: Under the PD condition, neuronal activity in the GPi and STN is increased but synchronization in the GPe and PPN is enhanced. β band oscillations are increased, and low-frequency activity in the PPN is disrupted. Coherence analysis reveals frequency-dependent coupling between the PPN and basal ganglia during PD-related network states. Comparison of different DBS targets demonstrates distinct effects. Within our 5-Hz-resolution frequency sweep, STN-DBS broadly suppresses β oscillations and, at approximately 70 Hz, minimizes the deviation of both the δ and β bands from the healthy reference; PPN-DBS enhances δ band activity at low stimulation frequencies or suppresses β synchronization at high frequencies, but these two effects do not co-occur within a single frequency window; GPi-DBS yields a larger increase in δ band power relative to the PD baseline near 55 Hz and suppresses β power in the GPi and PPN, yet the STN β deviation remains elevated across the scanned frequencies. CONCLUSIONS: PD-related patho

papers.title: Objective Longitudinal Monitoring of Postural Stability and Gait During Neurorehabilitation: Clinical Application of Instrumented Posturography and Three-Dimensional Motion Analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Instrumented human-movement assessment can be integrated with neurological examination and clinical scales to objectify functional deficits and quantify rehabilitation-related change. We evaluated a diagnostic-integration pathway in which TecnoBody ProKin posturography and Xsens MVN Awinda gait analysis were embedded in routine hospital neurorehabilitation as objective functional-diagnostic and outcome-monitoring tools. METHODS: This manuscript reports a secondary exploratory longitudinal analysis of prospectively acquired routine-care measurements. The publication dataset comprised 151 participants with baseline posturography (stroke, n = 90; Parkinson's disease, n = 38; multiple sclerosis [MS], n = 23); baseline gait data were available for 107. Diagnosis-specific Gaussian random-intercept models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with categorical time, and global time effects and PRE-to-POST contrasts were controlled using Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. RESULTS: In stroke, dynamic open-eye Total Stability Index (TSI) showed an FDR-significant global time effect (Wald χ2 CONCLUSIONS: Diagnostic integration of ProKin and Xsens into routine neurorehabilitation was feasible and generated objective patient-specific trajectories for balance and gait outcome monitoring. The measurements can objectify rehabilitation-related functional change, but the uncontrolled design does not establish causal treatment efficacy, and clinically meaningful individual-change thresholds remain to be validated.

papers.title: Green synthesis and chemical characterization of chitosan-pectin/Ag NPs and evaluation of their efficacy against Parkinsonian symptoms.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder driven by dopaminergic neurodegeneration, oxidative stress, and neuroinflammation. This study aimed to biosynthesize and evaluate immunomodulatory chitosan-pectin/silver nanoparticles (CHT-PCT/Ag NPs) using Umbilicaria esculenta extract as a green reducing and capping agent. METHODS: CHT-PCT/Ag NPs were synthesized via an eco-friendly approach wherein U. esculenta extract reduced AgNO3 RESULTS: The synthesized CHT-PCT/Ag NPs exhibited spherical morphology with an average dry size of 88.2 nm, a hydrodynamic diameter of 247.8 nm, and a stable zeta potential of + 24.5 ± 1.9 mV. The nanoformulation demonstrated pronounced radical-scavenging activity and favorable in vitro cytocompatibility. In MPTP-treated mice, CHT-PCT/Ag NPs significantly ameliorated motor deficits in pole and gait tasks. Biochemical, molecular, and histological assessments confirmed the preservation of dopaminergic neurons, marked reduction of oxidative and neuroinflammatory markers, and restoration of striatal dopamine metabolites. DISCUSSION & CONCLUSION: The neuroprotective performance of CHT-PCT/Ag NPs stems from the synergy between the stabilizing biopolymer shell and bioactive lichen phytoconstituents, which together attenuate oxidative cascades and neuroinflammation. Overall, green-synthesized CHT-PCT/Ag NPs offer a biocompatible, promising nanotherapeutic platform for Parkinson's disease management, warranting further pharmacokinetic and pathway-specific investigations.

papers.title: Feasibility and acceptability of the spatiotemporal activity modifications (STEAM) program: a Phase I clinical trial in people with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: The heterogeneous neuropathology, motor-cognitive deficits, and gait impairments in people with Parkinson's disease (PwP) present a need for more tailored rehabilitation. We conducted a preliminary phase I clinical trial to evaluate the feasibility and acceptability of the Spatiotemporal Activity Modification (STEAM) program, developed to address gait modulation deficits and motor-cognitive underpinnings in PwP. STEAM is an exercise-based rehabilitation program using a library of movement patterns to modify spatial features of gait (e.g., coordination of lower limb joints), temporal features of gait (e.g., movement timing and rhythm), or integrated spatiotemporal patterns. Participants with mild-moderate Parkinson's disease were randomized to either an isolated (ISO; n

papers.title: The Role of Autophagy in Aging and Longevity: A Comprehensive Review of Therapeutic Strategies to Modulate Autophagy and Promote Healthy Aging.
papers.abstract: Aging is associated with alterations in cellular homeostasis, including age-related dysregulation of autophagic capacity and flux. Autophagy is an essential catabolic process that clears damaged organelles and aggregated proteins; however, with age, changes in this process, including alterations in autophagosome formation, lysosomal degradation, selective autophagy, or the capacity to maintain autophagic flux under stress, may occur. These changes are implicated in the pathogenesis of diseases like Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and cancer. Autophagy is highly regulated by nutrition-sensing pathways, principally through the inhibitory action of mTORC1 (Mechanistic Target of Rapamycin Complex 1) and the activating role of AMPK (AMP-activated Protein Kinase). Consequently, strategies aimed at boosting autophagy hold significant potential, ranging from lifestyle modifications such as caloric restriction and exercise to pharmacological agents like rapamycin and metformin. Additionally, other natural compounds, such as spermidine and resveratrol, exhibit similar effects. By synthesizing the molecular mechanisms, regulatory networks, and therapeutic strategies, we highlight the critical importance of modulating autophagy to extend healthspan and develop targeted therapies against age-related decline.

papers.title: The Gut-Liver-Brain Axis in Neurodegeneration: Unraveling Metabolic-Immune Crosstalk from Peripheral Sensing to Central Vulnerability.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) have traditionally been regarded as brain-centered disorders driven primarily by the accumulation of pathological proteins. However, increasing evidence indicates that systemic metabolic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, intestinal dysbiosis, hepatic abnormalities, and barrier impairment may substantially influence disease susceptibility and progression. This review integrates current evidence on the gut-liver-brain axis (GLBA) and proposes Systemic Metabolic-Immune Reprogramming (SMIR) as a systems-level framework for understanding how peripheral disturbances may be translated into central nervous system vulnerability. Within this model, the gut generates microbial and metabolic signals, the liver functions as a metabolic-immune integrator that senses, transforms, buffers, or amplifies these signals, and the brain represents a downstream vulnerable organ in which persistent systemic disturbances reshape neuroimmune states and neuronal homeostasis. Particular emphasis is placed on the sequential and bidirectional interactions among intestinal barrier dysfunction, hepatic metabolic-immune activation, systemic inflammatory remodeling, blood-brain barrier vulnerability, and central neuroimmune dysregulation. Key molecular mediators include short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, tryptophan-kynurenine metabolites, trimethylamine N-oxide, ceramides, hepatokines, complement components, extracellular vesicles, and inflammatory cytokines, together with signaling pathways involving TLRs, FXR/TGR5, NLRP3, mitochondrial stress, and cGAS-STING. We further discuss how microglial and astrocytic metabolic reprogramming, mitochondrial dysfunction, ferroptosis, and impaired proteostasis may connect systemic metabolic stress with neuronal injury. papers.title: Temporal and spatial associations between mandatory grain fortification policy and noncommunicable disease burden in the United States: a population- and geography-based study.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The global spread of mandatory grain fortification with B vitamins and iron (GF) has been followed by escalating burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs). While prior studies linked GF to obesity and diabetes, its relationship with a broader NCD spectrum remains unclear. This study aimed to comprehensively describe the spatiotemporal associations between GF policy and NCD patterns in the United States (US) and to explore whether these associations are consistent with an international policy gradient. METHODS: Using US national data (1940-2020), we employed an ecological, longitudinal, and birth-cohort design. The exposure was the per capita availability of GF-related micronutrients (thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, iron). Outcomes included mortality from and prevalence of ischemic heart disease (IHD), ischemic stroke, cancer, diabetes, obesity, Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), asthma, congenital malformations, and life expectancy. We performed time-lag correlation and age-period-cohort analyses. To mitigate confounding by secular trends, we conducted a cross-national comparison of the US and the United Kingdom (UK) (both with long-term mandatory GF) versus France, Spain, Italy (Mediterranean nations without mandatory GF), and Japan (a high-income Asian nation with a rice-based diet without mandatory GF). RESULTS: The initiation of mandatory GF in the 1940s was followed by marked increases in mortality from IHD, ischemic stroke, diabetes, and cancer. Most states within the historical southern pellagra belt shifted from the lowest to the highest NCD burden, and this transition was associated with the lowest life expectancy. Black Americans-the subgroup with the highest dietary reliance on fortified staples-experienced a more rapid rise in cardiometabolic mortality than whites, reversing their pre‑fortification advantage in lower NCD burden. Congenital malformation mortality increased during the 1940s, with a notable peak in 1946-1947

papers.title: ENCORE: An End-to-End Pipeline to Reconstruct Enzyme-Constrained Metabolic Models for Microbial Communities and Identify Reporter Metabolites from Metagenomes.
papers.abstract: Microbial community Genome-scale Metabolic Models (Co-GEMs) capture cross-feeding interactions and provide insights into community-level metabolic activities. Enzyme-constrained GEMs (ecGEMs) incorporate enzyme abundance and kinetics to enable physiological simulations of species growth and cellular metabolism. However, an efficient framework for reconstructing microbial ecGEMs and integrating their metabolic exchange capabilities at the microbial community level is lacking. Therefore, we developed the ENzyme-constrained COmmunity REporter-metabolite pipeline (ENCORE), an integrated framework that reconstructs ecGEMs from metagenomic sequences and generates community-level microbe-metabolite interaction networks based on potential cross-feeding relationships. ENCORE identifies reporter metabolites reflecting microbial metabolic potential by incorporating microbial abundance profiles and mandatory exchange reactions. Gut metagenomic and blood metabolomic data of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients recruited from 2 Turkish cohorts were used for pipeline assessment and key metabolite discovery. The feasibility of ENCORE was assessed in 23 mild-to-moderate PD patients following 84 d of combined metabolic activators administration. ENCORE prioritized L-serine, the major combined metabolic activators compound, as a reporter metabolite, and 45% of the model metabolite-clinical metabolomics pairs showed concordant alterations. Its utility was further assessed in a larger cohort of 26 mild and 18 moderate PD patients to investigate microbiome-driven metabolic changes during PD progression. Identified reporter metabolites were significantly enriched in multiple metabolic pathways, most of which were involved in carbon metabolism. Collectively, ENCORE characterizes microbial metabolic potential and prioritizes key metabolites and associated taxa across perturbations and disease conditions. With further validation and refinement, it may complement clinical metabolomics and suppor

papers.title: Emerging Therapeutic Strategies Targeting Muscle Wasting in Parkinson's Disease: From Sarcopenia to Cachexia-like Syndrome.
papers.abstract: Clinically relevant muscle wasting affects a substantial proportion of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), although its prevalence varies according to the diagnostic criteria applied. This condition accelerates disease progression, reduces quality of life, and is a poor prognostic indicator associated with increased disability and mortality. Despite its clinical relevance, the molecular mechanisms underlying muscle wasting remain underinvestigated and poorly understood, constituting an unmet clinical need. Currently, there is insufficient evidence to definitively establish PD-associated muscle wasting as true cachexia, a syndrome characterized by systemic inflammation and metabolic dysregulation. Moreover, distinguishing the contribution of age-related sarcopenia from PD-specific pathological mechanisms remains challenging. A deeper understanding of the pathways and molecular signals involved in PD-associated muscle wasting may lead to therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes. Given the multifactorial nature of PD muscle wasting-e.g., motor neuron degeneration, aging, oxidative stress, inflammation, protein degradation, mitochondrial dysfunction-our aim is to provide a comprehensive overview of the current data on the cellular, molecular, and systemic mechanisms involved in this process. We also identify emerging therapeutic targets that may help prevent, attenuate, or reverse muscle atrophy in PD. Understanding muscle-brain crosstalk may help redefine PD as a systemic rather than neurodegenerative disorder.
